title: Motivating productive effort through testing
author: Matthew Evans
summary: Matthew Evans argues that the main purpose of testing students is not to find out what they know but to improve learning, and one of the ways tests do this is by motivating productive effort. Drawing on seven psychological theories -- expectancy-value, attribution, self-efficacy, interest, achievement goal, and social norms theory among them -- he identifies seven distinct reasons students choose to study for a test, from past success and correct attribution to identifying as a "successful student" and wanting to belong to a successful group. For each reason he offers concrete classroom moves: using low-stakes, high-success-rate tests to build expectancy; narrating success as linked to effort rather than ability; building self-efficacy through explicit study strategies rather than generic study-skills programmes; and creating positive group norms around productive study. Evans is careful to distinguish productive effort (initiating, attending to the right things, using an effective approach, and persisting) from mere motivation, arguing teachers must build both a student's will to study and their capacity to study effectively. He closes with practical guidance for before, during, and after a test, all oriented around treating results as information for the student's ongoing mastery rather than a verdict on their ability.
points: Evans distinguishes productive effort from motivation: teachers must build both a student's volition to study (initiate, persist) and their capacity to study effectively (attend to the right things, use good methods).

Achievement goal theory suggests students with mastery goals outperform those with performance goals over time, which means teachers should portray tests as checkpoints toward mastery rather than comparative rankings.

Self-efficacy for test preparation is domain-specific, so a generic study-skills programme won't build it -- teachers need to be explicit about how to study this specific topic for this specific type of test.
Evans recommends teachers avoid comparisons between students after a test and instead narrate success as the direct result of productive study behaviours, reinforcing correct attribution.
quotes: The main reason for testing students is to improve learning, and one of the ways tests do this is to motivate productive effort by students – studying!
These folk theories can serve to place responsibility for effort with the student and their circumstances and not with the teacher.
For a student’s action to be productive in relation to test preparation, the student must: Initiate study. Pay attention to the right things. Adopt an effective approach to study. Persist to study.
Students are more likely to work for something they perceive they have a good chance of succeeding in.
Achievement goal theory suggests that students who adopt mastery goals, that is those that aim to master the subject rather than perform well in tests, will achieve more in the long term.
Remember, the main reason for testing students is to improve learning. Motivating productive effort through testing is a key competence for teachers.
